per_question.question: Lambda SnapStart and provisioned concurrency both exist to reduce cold-start latency, but you can't enable both on the same function version. Using what each mechanism actually does, explain why they're mutually exclusive and which runtimes get the free option.

per_question.generated_answer:
Lambda SnapStart and provisioned concurrency both aim to reduce cold-start latency, but they work in different ways and are mutually exclusive because they cannot be used together on the same function version.

Lambda SnapStart uses cached snapshots of the execution environment to significantly improve startup performance. This means that the execution environment is already set up and ready to go, reducing the time it takes to start the function.

Provisioned concurrency, on the other hand, pre-initializes a certain number of execution environments ahead of time, so that they are prepared to respond immediately to function requests. This also reduces cold-start latency.

However, these two mechanisms cannot be used together because they require different levels of initialization. If a function is using provisioned concurrency, it means that the execution environment is already pre-initialized, and using SnapStart would be redundant. Similarly, if a function is using SnapStart, it means that the execution environment is already set up, and using provisioned concurrency would be unnecessary.

The .NET runtime gets the free option, as it employs lazy compilation and initialization for each library that your code calls for the first time. This means that the first invocation of a Lambda function might take longer than subsequent ones, but using the `AWS_LAMBDA_DOTNET_PREJIT` environment variable can improve the latency for functions, even if they don't use provisioned concurrency.

Because both are alternative solutions to the same cold-start problem, Lambda doesn't allow configuring them together on one function version. SnapStart is available at no extra cost for the Java 11 and Java 17 runtimes, while provisioned concurrency incurs additional charges regardless of runtime.
